Decompose model implied variance into between person, process and measurement

Source: R/ctVarianceDecomposition.R
ctVarianceDecomposition.Rd

Splits the variance each indicator of a fitted model implies into a between person part, a within person part from the latent process, and a within person part from measurement error. The process part is further split into the contribution of the system noise and that of the mean path changing over time.

Usage

ctVarianceDecomposition(
  fit,
  method = c("auto", "moment", "simulation"),
  persons = c("auto", "model", "estimated"),
  scale = c("latent", "response"),
  times = NULL,
  npersons = 200L,
  npaths = 20L,
  latents = TRUE,
  quadpoints = 21L,
  subjects = "all",
  realid = TRUE,
  sources = NULL
)

Arguments

fit

fit object as generated by ctFit, from either backend.

method

How the model implied moments are computed. 'moment' uses the forward moment recursion, which is exact and needs linear dynamics. 'simulation' draws trajectories with the julia engine, for models with state dependent DRIFT or DIFFUSION cells. 'auto', the default, uses 'moment' unless the model has such cells.

persons

Which persons the between person variance refers to. 'model' draws persons from the fitted population distribution of the random effects. 'estimated' uses the subjects in the data. On a backend='julia' fit each subject is represented by its estimated effects plus a draw from their posterior. On a stan fit each subject is represented by its estimated (empirical Bayes) matrices, which understates the between person variance. 'auto', the default, uses 'model' for julia fits and 'estimated' for stan fits, and says which it used.

scale

For a binary or ordinal indicator, whether to decompose the linear predictor behind the logit ('latent', the default, with a measurement variance of \(\pi^2/3\)) or the observed response ('response', integrating the link over each row's normal distribution). The two are the same for a Gaussian indicator.

times

If given, decompose at each of these times. By default the decomposition averages over each person's observation times. Either a numeric vector, or 'asdata' for the observed occasions. Every person is evaluated at the same times. The result gains a time column and has no within.deterministic column, since that term is the variance of the mean path over time. Not available with method='simulation' or with time dependent predictors.

npersons

Number of persons to draw when persons='model'. With persons='estimated' on a julia fit, each subject gets enough draws to make at least this many persons in total.

npaths

Trajectories drawn per person when method='simulation'. The result is unbiased for any npaths, but small values give noisy results.

latents

If TRUE, also decompose the latent processes, which have no measurement component.

quadpoints

Gauss-Hermite nodes used when scale='response'.

subjects

'all', or the subjects whose designs the decomposition is computed over, as ids in the data (see realid).

realid

If TRUE (the default), subjects are read as the ids in the data, and integers that are not ids there are read as ctsem's numbering of the subjects, 1 to N, with a message. If FALSE, they are read as that numbering.

sources

Optional named list of latent names, one entry per group of processes whose innovations are independent of the other groups, such as fast affect, a daily process and a slow process. The stochastic within person term is then split by source, into within.stochastic.<group> for each group's innovations and within.stochastic.initial for what remains of the initial state variance. These add up to within.stochastic. When averaging over the observation times, level.<group> gives the part of each group's term that is variance in a person's average level over their record. This shows how much a slow process acts as a stable level within the record. Needs method='moment'.

Value

A data frame of class ctVarianceDecomposition, one row per variable, with columns variable, type, between, within.deterministic, within.stochastic, within.measurement, within, total and the corresponding proportions. The population the between column refers to, the scale, and the number of persons are recorded as attributes and shown by print.

Details

The decomposition applies the law of total variance over the (person, occasion) pairs in the design of the fit. With \(g = E[y | \eta]\) the expected observation given the latent state,

$$Var(y) = E[Var(y|\eta)] + E_i E_t Var(g) + E_i Var_t(E[g]) + Var_i(E[g])$$

and the four terms are the four columns reported. They are non-negative and sum to the total.

within.deterministic is the variance of a person's mean path over their observation times. It is zero for a stationary process without time dependent predictors, and positive when there is a trend, a shift due to a predictor, or a process that has not settled from its initial distribution.

The moments are computed over each subject's observation times without using the observed values, so unequal spacing, missing observations and time dependent predictors are all accounted for. The result is exact for models with linear dynamics. For a model whose DRIFT or DIFFUSION depends on the state, method='moment' is refused, and method='simulation' applies the same decomposition to simulated trajectories. State dependent measurement cells (LAMBDA, MANIFESTMEANS, MANIFESTVAR) are not supported by either method.

Random effect levels. A model with a grouping level above the subject (id = c('subject','study') in ctModel), fitted with intoverpop='laplace' or sampled, gets one between.<level> column per level. Each is the variance of that level's departure from the level above it, and together they sum to between. Estimated random effects are shrunk towards the level above, more strongly where a unit has little data, so persons='estimated' adds to each estimate a draw from that unit's posterior.

When the split changes over time. The columns are averages over each person's occasions. For a process that has not settled the split differs between occasions, and within.deterministic is then large. Use times to see the split at each time.

Designs. Each person is evaluated at their own observation times, so balanced and unbalanced designs and missing observations are all handled, and the result does not depend on which observations are missing. Persons are weighted equally, however many observations each has.

With method='simulation', the function checks that the engine draws the individually varying parameters, and stops with an error if it does not.

See also

ctSummaryMatrices for the matrices this is built from, and ctStateDependencePlot for a model whose dynamics vary over the state space.

Examples

# \donttest{
ctVarianceDecomposition(ctstantestfit)
# }
